lessons.title: Understanding Fertilizer Grades (N-P-K)
lessons.body:
Fertilizer grades are three numbers on a bag, like 20-10-10. They tell you the percentage of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P as P2O5), and potassium (K as K2O) in the bag. So a 50 kg bag of 20-10-10 contains 10 kg N, 5 kg P2O5, and 5 kg K2O. The rest is filler like sand or limestone. In Africa, common grades include 23-21-0+4S for maize in Kenya, 12-24-12 for cotton in Burkina Faso, and 15-15-15 for general use. Knowing the grade helps you choose the right fertilizer for your crop and soil.

To calculate nutrients per bag, multiply the grade percentage by the bag weight. For a 50 kg bag of 20-10-10: N = 20% of 50 = 10 kg; P2O5 = 10% of 50 = 5 kg; K2O = 10% of 50 = 5 kg. If a farmer needs 120 kg N per hectare, and uses 20-10-10, he needs 120 / 0.20 = 600 kg of fertilizer per hectare. Thatâs 12 bags of 50 kg. But that also gives 60 kg P2O5 and 60 kg K2O, which may be too much or too little depending on soil tests.

Grades can be customized. For example, a blend for maize in Tanzania might be 25-10-10+5S+1Zn. The extra S and Zn are secondary and micronutrients. Always check the label for other nutrients. In West Africa, 15-15-15 is common, but for rice, 20-10-10 is preferred. The grade is the foundation of any blend formulation.

When you blend, you mix raw materials like urea (46-0-0), diammonium phosphate (18-46-0), and muriate of potash (0-0-60) to achieve a target grade. For example, to make 1000 kg of 20-10-10, you need 200 kg N, 100 kg P2O5, and 100 kg K2O. Using urea, DAP, and MOP: urea provides 46% N, DAP provides 18% N and 46% P2O5, MOP provides 60% K2O. You solve for amounts. This lesson sets the stage for calculations.

Remember: N-P-K numbers are always in that order. A bag labeled 0-0-60 is just potassium. A bag labeled 46-0-0 is urea. Knowing this prevents costly mistakes. In Africa, where fertilizer is expensive, accurate grade understanding saves money and increases yields.

lessons.title: Calculating Nutrient Contributions from Raw Materials
lessons.body:
Raw materials are the ingredients you mix to make a blend. Each has a nutrient analysis. Common ones: Urea (46-0-0), Ammonium Sulphate (21-0-0+24S), DAP (18-46-0), Monoammonium Phosphate (MAP) (11-52-0), Muriate of Potash (MOP) (0-0-60), Sulphate of Potash (SOP) (0-0-50+18S), Triple Superphosphate (TSP) (0-46-0), and limestone filler (0-0-0). To calculate how much nutrient a raw material contributes, multiply its nutrient percentage by the amount used. For example, 100 kg of urea gives 46 kg N. 100 kg of DAP gives 18 kg N and 46 kg P2O5.

Suppose you want to make 1000 kg of a blend. You decide to use 300 kg DAP, 200 kg MOP, 400 kg urea, and 100 kg filler. Calculate contributions: DAP: N = 0.18*300 = 54 kg; P2O5 = 0.46*300 = 138 kg. MOP: K2O = 0.60*200 = 120 kg. Urea: N = 0.46*400 = 184 kg. Total N = 54+184 = 238 kg; P2O5 = 138 kg; K2O = 120 kg. The grade would be 23.8-13.8-12.0. You can adjust to hit a target.

In Africa, raw materials vary. Local urea might be 46% N, but if it absorbs moisture, the actual N is lower. Always use the analysis on the bag. If you buy in bulk, ask for a certificate of analysis. For example, in Nigeria, DAP from Indorama may have 18% N and 46% P2O5. In Kenya, MOP from Israel is 60% K2O. Use these values.

To calculate nutrient contributions for a target grade, set up equations. For 1000 kg of 20-10-10, you need 200 kg N, 100 kg P2O5, 100 kg K2O. Let x = kg urea, y = kg DAP, z = kg MOP, and filler = 1000 - x - y - z. From P2O5: 0.46y = 100 => y = 217.4 kg. From K2O: 0.60z = 100 => z = 166.7 kg. From N: 0.46x + 0.18y = 200 => 0.46x + 0.18*217.4 = 200 => 0.46x + 39.1 = 200 => 0.46x = 160.9 => x = 349.8 kg. Filler = 1000 - 349.8 - 217.4 - 166.7 = 266.1 kg. So you need 349.8 kg urea, 217.4 kg DAP, 166.7 kg MOP, and 266.1 kg filler. This is the core calculation.

Always check that totals make sense. If a raw material provides two nutrients, like DAP, it affects both N and P. Thatâs why you solve for P first, then N. Practice with different raw materials and targets. In Africa, where filler may be sand or rice husk, ensure it doesnât add nutrients. Use a calculator or spreadsheet to avoid errors.

lessons.title: Balancing Formulations Using Algebraic Methods
lessons.body:
Algebra helps you find the right amounts of raw materials to hit a target grade. You set up equations based on nutrient requirements. For a 1000 kg blend of target grade N-P-K, you need N kg N, P kg P2O5, K kg K2O. Let x, y, z be the amounts of three raw materials. Each raw material has known percentages. For example, urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), MOP (0-0-60). You write: 0.46x + 0.18y = N (from N), 0.46y = P (from P2O5), 0.60z = K (from K2O). Solve for y from P, then z from K, then x from N. Then filler = 1000 - x - y - z.

If you have more than three raw materials, you have more variables. You can fix some amounts based on availability or cost. For example, you might want to use 100 kg of ammonium sulphate for sulphur. Then adjust others. The algebra becomes a system of linear equations. You can solve by substitution or elimination. In Africa, where raw materials may be limited, you often use whatâs available. For instance, if you donât have MOP, you might use SOP (0-0-50) but then you get sulphur. Adjust equations accordingly.

Example: Target 15-15-15, 1000 kg. Need 150 kg N, 150 kg P2O5, 150 kg K2O. Use urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), MOP (0-0-60). From P: 0.46y = 150 => y = 326.1 kg. From K: 0.60z = 150 => z = 250 kg. From N: 0.46x + 0.18*326.1 = 150 => 0.46x + 58.7 = 150 => 0.46x = 91.3 => x = 198.5 kg. Filler = 1000 - 198.5 - 326.1 - 250 = 225.4 kg. Check: N from urea = 91.3, from DAP = 58.7, total = 150. Good.

If you want to use TSP (0-46-0) instead of DAP, then you have no N from P source. Equations: 0.46x = 150 => x = 326.1 kg urea. 0.46y = 150 => y = 326.1 kg TSP. 0.60z = 150 => z = 250 kg MOP. Filler = 1000 - 326.1 - 326.1 - 250 = 97.8 kg. That works, but you use more urea and TSP. Cost may differ.

Always check that all amounts are positive. If a solution gives negative, you need to change raw materials or target. In Africa, where soil deficiencies vary, you might need to adjust grades. For example, for maize in Malawi, a common blend is 23-21-0+4S. You would use urea, DAP, and ammonium sulphate. Set up equations: N from urea + N from DAP + N from AS = 230 kg (for 1000 kg). P from DAP = 210 kg. S from AS = 40 kg. Solve. This algebraic method is the backbone of custom blending.

lessons.title: Using Software and Spreadsheets for Formulation
lessons.body:
Manual calculations are good, but software speeds things up and reduces errors. In Africa, many blenders use Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets. You can set up a simple spreadsheet: columns for raw materials, their nutrient percentages, and the amount you plan to use. Then formulas calculate total N, P, K. You can use 'Solver' add-in to find amounts that meet a target grade at minimum cost. For example, in Excel, set target cells for N, P, K, and use Solver to adjust raw material amounts. This is powerful for optimizing cost.

Another tool is the 'Fertilizer Blending Calculator' app available on Android. It lets you input target grade and raw materials, and it gives you the mix. Some apps are free, like 'Fertilizer Blend Calculator' by AgriApp. In Kenya, the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) has developed a fertilizer advisory tool. In Nigeria, the Fertilizer Producers and Suppliers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN) offers blending software. These tools often include local raw material analyses.

For a beginner, start with a spreadsheet. Create a table: A1: Raw Material, B1: %N, C1: %P2O5, D1: %K2O, E1: Amount (kg). Then in F1: =B2*E2/100 for N contribution. Sum down. Use 'Goal Seek' to adjust one amount to hit a target. For example, if you want 200 kg N, and you have urea and DAP, set total N cell to 200 by changing urea amount. But Goal Seek only changes one cell. For multiple, use Solver.

In Africa, internet may be limited, so offline tools are useful. You can download a template from websites like www.fertilizer.org. Or use a simple calculator. Remember, software is only as good as the data. Always input accurate nutrient analyses from your supplier. If you buy urea from a local dealer, test it or ask for a lab report. Garbage in, garbage out.

Training: Many agricultural extension officers in Africa can help you set up a spreadsheet. In Ethiopia, the Agricultural Transformation Agency (ATA) has soil fertility maps and fertilizer recommendations. You can use their data to set targets. Also, smartphone apps like 'Plantwise' have fertilizer calculators. Practice with a known example: 1000 kg of 20-10-10 using urea, DAP, MOP. See if your spreadsheet matches manual calculation. Once set up, you can quickly test different raw materials and prices. This saves time and money.

lessons.title: Adjusting for Moisture and Impurities
lessons.body:
Raw materials are not pure. Urea absorbs moisture from the air, so a bag labeled 46% N might actually contain 45% N if itâs been exposed. DAP can have impurities like iron or aluminum. Moisture also adds weight but no nutrients. If you formulate based on 1000 kg of raw materials, but they contain 5% moisture, you actually have only 950 kg of dry matter. So your nutrient content is lower. To adjust, you need to calculate on a dry basis. For example, if urea has 2% moisture, then 100 kg of urea contains 98 kg dry urea. The N content is 46% of dry urea, so actual N = 0.46 * 98 = 45.08 kg. So you need slightly more urea to hit target N.

Impurities can also affect nutrient analysis. For instance, TSP may contain 46% P2O5, but if it has 3% iron, the P2O5 might be 44%. Always use the actual analysis from a lab. In Africa, where storage can be poor, moisture is a big issue. In humid areas like the Congo Basin, urea can cake and absorb up to 5% moisture. In dry areas like the Sahel, moisture is less of a problem but dust and sand can contaminate.

To adjust, first determine moisture content. You can use a moisture meter, or dry a sample in an oven. For a quick field test, weigh a sample, dry it in the sun or with a hair dryer, and weigh again. The weight loss is moisture. Then calculate dry matter. For each raw material, adjust the amount used: actual amount = (desired dry amount) / (1 - moisture%). For example, if you need 100 kg dry urea and it has 2% moisture, you need 100 / 0.98 = 102.04 kg wet urea. Then the N contribution is 0.46 * 100 = 46 kg N (since dry basis). So you still get the target.

Impurities: If a raw material has a lower nutrient analysis than labeled, you must use more. For example, if DAP is labeled 18-46-0 but analysis shows 17-44-0, then you need to recalculate. Use the actual percentages. In many African countries, fertilizer quality is regulated, but enforcement varies. Always buy from reputable dealers. If you blend, test your raw materials. Simple lab tests: for N, use Kjeldahl method; for P, spectrophotometer; for K, flame photometer. These may not be available, so use a mobile lab or send to a national lab.

Adjusting for moisture and impurities ensures your final blend meets the guaranteed grade. If you ignore it, farmers may under-apply nutrients. For example, a 50 kg bag of 20-10-10 should have 10 kg N. If moisture is 3%, you might only have 9.7 kg N. Thatâs a 3% loss. Over a hectare, thatâs significant. So always account for moisture and impurities in your formulation calculations.

lessons.title: Case Studies: Formulating Common Blends
lessons.body:
Case Study 1: Maize blend in Kenya. Target: 23-21-0+4S for 1000 kg. Raw materials: Urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), Ammonium Sulphate (21-0-0+24S), and filler. Need 230 kg N, 210 kg P2O5, 40 kg S. From P: DAP provides 46% P2O5, so y = 210 / 0.46 = 456.5 kg DAP. From S: AS provides 24% S, so z = 40 / 0.24 = 166.7 kg AS. N from DAP = 0.18*456.5 = 82.2 kg. N from AS = 0.21*166.7 = 35.0 kg. Total N so far = 117.2 kg. Need 230 kg, so remaining N = 112.8 kg from urea. Urea amount = 112.8 / 0.46 = 245.2 kg. Filler = 1000 - 456.5 - 166.7 - 245.2 = 131.6 kg. Check: N from urea = 112.8, total N = 82.2+35.0+112.8 = 230. Good. This blend is used in Kenyaâs maize belt.

Case Study 2: Rice blend in Nigeria. Target: 20-10-10 for 1000 kg. Raw materials: Urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), MOP (0-0-60), filler. Need 200 kg N, 100 kg P2O5, 100 kg K2O. From P: DAP = 100 / 0.46 = 217.4 kg. From K: MOP = 100 / 0.60 = 166.7 kg. N from DAP = 0.18*217.4 = 39.1 kg. Remaining N = 160.9 kg from urea => urea = 160.9 / 0.46 = 349.8 kg. Filler = 1000 - 217.4 - 166.7 - 349.8 = 266.1 kg. This blend is common in Nigeriaâs rice paddies.

Case Study 3: Cotton blend in Burkina Faso. Target: 12-24-12 for 1000 kg. Raw materials: Urea (46-0-0), TSP (0-46-0), MOP (0-0-60), filler. Need 120 kg N, 240 kg P2O5, 120 kg K2O. From P: TSP = 240 / 0.46 = 521.7 kg. From K: MOP = 120 / 0.60 = 200 kg. From N: urea = 120 / 0.46 = 260.9 kg. Filler = 1000 - 521.7 - 200 - 260.9 = 17.4 kg. This blend is used in Burkina Fasoâs cotton zones.

Case Study 4: Tea blend in Malawi. Target: 25-5-5+5S for 1000 kg. Raw materials: Urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), Ammonium Sulphate (21-0-0+24S), MOP (0-0-60), filler. Need 250 kg N, 50 kg P2O5, 50 kg K2O, 50 kg S. From P: DAP = 50 / 0.46 = 108.7 kg. From K: MOP = 50 / 0.60 = 83.3 kg. From S: AS = 50 / 0.24 = 208.3 kg. N from DAP = 0.18*108.7 = 19.6 kg. N from AS = 0.21*208.3 = 43.7 kg. Total N so far = 63.3 kg. Remaining N = 186.7 kg from urea => urea = 186.7 / 0.46 = 405.9 kg. Filler = 1000 - 108.7 - 83.3 - 208.3 - 405.9 = 193.8 kg. This blend is used in Malawiâs tea estates.

These case studies show how to apply the algebraic method to real African crops. Always verify with a lab test after blending. Adjust for moisture and impurities as needed. With practice, you can formulate any blend.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Blend Formulation in African Agribusiness

Fertilizer blending is a commercial activity before it is a technical one. In Africa, the blender's margin depends on buying the right raw materials at the right price, hitting the guaranteed grade consistently, and avoiding costly rework, penalties, and customer complaints. This practical reference consolidates the numbers, tables, and rules of thumb that a blender, agronomist, or input dealer needs on the shop floor. It complements the six lessons in this module and is written for the reality of African supply chains: variable raw material quality, imported intermediates, small batch sizes, and buyers who test what you sell.

Why Formulation Precision Is a Business Issue

A fertilizer grade such as 20-10-10 means the product guarantees 20% nitrogen (N), 10% phosphorus (expressed as P2O5), and 10% potassium (expressed as K2O) by weight. In most African markets, grades are regulated and enforced through national fertilizer control systems. If your blend is under-grade, you face rejected deliveries, regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, and possible litigation. If you are over-grade, you are giving away nutrients for free and eroding margin. Both errors are expensive; the target is to land inside the guaranteed tolerance, not to "aim high for safety."

Blending is also a sourcing decision. A blender in Kenya buying urea, DAP, MOP, and filler must decide how much of each to purchase based on the formulation, the cost per kg of nutrient, and the availability of local versus imported materials. That is why this lesson is framed around money: every percentage point of nutrient is a cost, and every formulation decision is a purchasing decision.

Raw Material Nutrient Contents: The Numbers You Actually Use

Every formulation starts from the nutrient analysis of the raw materials on hand. The table below gives typical values for the intermediates most commonly traded in Africa. Always confirm with the supplier's certificate of analysis (CoA) because imported lots vary, especially in moisture and granule size.

Table 1: Typical nutrient content of common fertilizer raw materials (% by weight)
MaterialN (%)P2O5 (%)K2O (%)Notes
Urea (46-0-0)4600Highly hygroscopic; store dry
Ammonium sulphate (21-0-0)2100Supplies sulphur; acidifying
Calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN, 27-0-0)2700Regulated in some countries
DAP (18-46-0)18460Main P source
MAP (12-61-0)12610High-analysis P
Triple superphosphate (TSP, 0-46-0)0460No N
Muriate of potash (MOP, 0-0-60)0060Main K source
Sulphate of potash (SOP, 0-0-50)0050For chloride-sensitive crops
NPK compound (e.g., 23-21-0)23210Used as a base in blends

Sources: Values are typical guaranteed analyses for internationally traded grades as listed in FAO (2006), Plant Nutrition for Food Security, and the International Fertilizer Association (IFA) IFASTAT product definitions. Confirm actual lot analysis with supplier CoA before formulation.

Worked Formulation: 20-10-10 per 1,000 kg Batch

This is the classic African cereal and maize blend. Using urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), and MOP (0-0-60), with filler to make up the balance:

  1. Phosphorus first: 1000 kg Ã 10% P2O5 = 100 kg P2O5. DAP needed = 100 Ã· 0.46 = 217.4 kg. This also brings N: 217.4 Ã 0.18 = 39.1 kg N.
  2. Potassium next: 1000 Ã 10% K2O = 100 kg K2O. MOP needed = 100 Ã· 0.60 = 166.7 kg.
  3. Nitrogen balance: target 200 kg N. Already supplied 39.1 kg from DAP, so need 160.9 kg from urea. Urea = 160.9 Ã· 0.46 = 349.8 kg.
  4. Filler: 1000 â (217.4 + 166.7 + 349.8) = 266.1 kg filler (e.g., sand, limestone, or a neutral carrier).

Check: 349.8 + 217.4 + 166.7 + 266.1 = 1000 kg. N = (349.8Ã0.46) + (217.4Ã0.18) = 160.9 + 39.1 = 200 kg = 20%. Correct.

Table 2: Batch sheet for 1,000 kg of 20-10-10 (worked example)

MOP (0-0-60)166.716.700100.0

Source: Author's calculation using standard algebraic formulation method as described in FAO (2006) and the IFDC Fertilizer Blending Manual (IFDC, Muscle Shoals).

Moisture, Impurities, and the Real-World Correction

On paper the numbers balance. In the warehouse they do not, because raw materials carry moisture and impurities that dilute nutrients. If your urea is 2% moisture, then 1,000 kg of as-received urea contains only 980 kg of dry urea, and the nutrient contribution drops by 2%. The practical correction is to adjust the batch factor upward: divide the calculated dry weight by (1 â moisture fraction). For 349.8 kg of urea at 2% moisture, use 349.8 Ã· 0.98 = 356.9 kg as-received. Apply the same logic to each material.

Impurities such as sand, clay, or coating residues also reduce nutrient density. If a supplier's DAP is 97% pure, the effective P2O5 is 46 Ã 0.97 = 44.6%, not 46%. Over a 1,000 kg batch, that difference is 3 kg of P2O5 â enough to fail a tolerance test. Build a "purity factor" into your spreadsheet and update it every time a new lot arrives.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Do Not Ignore

Fertilizer blending involves dust, corrosive salts, and in the case of ammonium nitrateâbased materials, explosion and fire risk. Never blend ammonium nitrate (AN) or CAN with combustible organic fillers, and never use a mixer that has previously handled incompatible materials without a full clean-down. Urea and AN must not be stored together or blended together in some jurisdictions. Always wear dust masks, eye protection, and gloves; ensure ventilation; and ground all equipment to prevent static ignition. Follow national regulations (e.g., Kenya's OSHA 2007, South Africa's OHS Act, and national fertilizer control acts) and the supplier's safety data sheets (SDS). If in doubt, stop and consult your regulator before blending.

Spreadsheet and Software Shortcuts

For routine blends, a simple spreadsheet with columns for material, analysis, target nutrient, required kg, moisture factor, and as-received kg is enough. Free and low-cost tools used across Africa include the IFDC/FAO nutrient balance sheets, the "Fertilizer Blending Calculator" templates distributed by national agricultural research systems, and commercial ERP modules in larger plants. The key is to lock the formulas so that a single change in target grade recalculates the whole batch sheet, and to add a validation column that flags when the total exceeds 1,000 kg or when a nutrient is under target.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Confirm the target grade and the national tolerance limits before you start (e.g., Â±0.5% or as regulated).
  • Obtain a certificate of analysis (CoA) for every raw material lot; record moisture, purity, and granule size.
  • Calculate P and K requirements first, then balance N â this avoids over-supplying N from DAP/MAP.
  • Apply moisture and purity correction factors to convert dry-basis weights to as-received weights.
  • Check that the sum of all components equals the batch size; adjust filler last.
  • Sample and test the finished blend before bagging; retain a sample for at least the shelf life.
  • Verify compatibility: never blend AN/CAN with urea, organic matter, or incompatible fillers.
  • Record the batch number, date, raw material lots, and operator for traceability and regulatory audits.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Plant Nutrition for Food Security: A Guide for Integrated Nutrient Management (Fertilizer and Plant Nutrition Bulletin 16), available at fao.org.
  • FAO â Fertilizer and Plant Nutrition Bulletins series, fao.org/soils-portal.
  • International Fertilizer Association (IFA) â IFASTAT and fertilizer product definitions, ifastat.org.
  • IFDC â Fertilizer Blending Manual and related technical resources, ifdc.org.
  • African Fertilizer and Agribusiness Partnership (AFAP) â country fertilizer regulations and market reports, afap-partnership.org.

Note: This lesson is a practical reference and does not replace national fertilizer regulations or professional agronomic advice. Always verify grades, tolerances, and safety requirements with the relevant national authority before commercial blending.

quiz.q: What does a fertilizer grade of 20-10-10 mean?
quiz.explanation: The grade numbers represent the percentage of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P2O5), and potassium (K2O) in that order.

quiz.q: How many kg of N are in a 50 kg bag of 20-10-10?
quiz.explanation: 20% of 50 kg is 10 kg N.

quiz.q: Which raw material provides only nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Urea is 46-0-0, so it provides only nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is the P2O5 content in 100 kg of DAP (18-46-0)?
quiz.explanation: DAP is 46% P2O5, so 100 kg contains 46 kg P2O5.

quiz.q: To make 1000 kg of 15-15-15 using urea, DAP, and MOP, how much DAP is needed?
In the algebraic method, which nutrient equation is solved first when using DAP?
quiz.explanation: DAP is the only source of P2O5, so you solve for phosphorus first to find DAP amount.

quiz.q: What is the role of filler in a blend?
options: B) Makes up weight without adding nutrients
quiz.explanation: Filler like sand or limestone is used to reach the desired total weight without adding N, P, or K.

quiz.q: If a raw material has 5% moisture, how much wet material is needed to get 100 kg dry material?
quiz.explanation: Wet amount = dry amount / (1 - moisture%) = 100 / 0.95 = 105.3 kg.

quiz.q: Which software tool can be used to optimize fertilizer blends?
quiz.explanation: Excel Solver can adjust raw material amounts to meet target nutrients at minimum cost.

quiz.q: What is a common maize blend in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: 23-21-0+4S is a common maize blend in Kenya, especially for the maize belt.

quiz.q: How many kg of K2O are in 200 kg of MOP (0-0-60)?
quiz.explanation: MOP is 60% K2O, so 200 kg * 0.60 = 120 kg K2O.

quiz.q: In a 1000 kg blend of 20-10-10, how much N is needed?
quiz.explanation: 20% of 1000 kg is 200 kg N.

quiz.q: Which raw material provides both N and P2O5?
quiz.explanation: DAP (18-46-0) provides both nitrogen and phosphorus.

quiz.q: What is the first step in adjusting for moisture?
quiz.explanation: You must first measure or estimate the moisture content of each raw material.

quiz.q: If urea has 2% moisture, how much actual N is in 100 kg wet urea?
Which of these is a secondary nutrient often included in blends?
quiz.explanation: Sulphur (S) is a secondary nutrient, while zinc, boron, and copper are micronutrients.

quiz.q: In the case study for rice in Nigeria, what is the target grade?
quiz.explanation: The rice blend case study in Nigeria targets 20-10-10.

quiz.q: How much MOP is needed for 1000 kg of 12-24-12?
quiz.explanation: K2O needed = 120 kg; MOP = 120 / 0.60 = 200 kg.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of using ammonium sulphate in a blend?
quiz.explanation: Ammonium sulphate (21-0-0+24S) provides both nitrogen and sulphur.

quiz.q: Which method is used to solve for multiple raw materials in a blend?
quiz.explanation: Algebraic equations (linear equations) are used to solve for amounts of raw materials.

quiz.q: In Excel, which tool adjusts multiple cells to meet a target?
quiz.explanation: Solver can adjust multiple cells, while Goal Seek only adjusts one.

quiz.q: What is a common filler material in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sand or limestone is often used as filler because it is cheap and adds no nutrients.

quiz.q: If a blend requires 150 kg P2O5 and you use TSP (0-46-0), how much TSP is needed?
What is the N content in 100 kg of ammonium sulphate (21-0-0)?
quiz.explanation: Ammonium sulphate is 21% N, so 100 kg contains 21 kg N.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check for impurities in raw materials?
quiz.explanation: Impurities dilute the nutrient concentration, so you may need more raw material to hit target.

quiz.q: In the Malawi tea blend case study, what is the target grade?
quiz.explanation: The tea blend in Malawi targets 25-5-5+5S.

quiz.q: How much urea is needed for 1000 kg of 20-10-10 using urea, DAP, MOP?
quiz.explanation: From the example, urea = 349.8 kg.

quiz.q: What is the K2O content in 100 kg of SOP (0-0-50)?
quiz.explanation: SOP is 50% K2O, so 100 kg contains 50 kg K2O.

quiz.q: Which of these is a real tool for fertilizer blending in Africa?
quiz.explanation: KALRO in Kenya has developed a fertilizer advisory tool for blending.

quiz.q: If you need 40 kg S and use ammonium sulphate (24% S), how much AS is needed?
